title: Never Whistle at Night in Korea or Japan #shorts
description_hook: In Korea and Japan, one sound after dark is said to invite things into your house.

lines.say: Rule one. In Korea and Japan, never whistle after dark.
lines.img: a teenage girl at an open apartment window at night, lips pursed as if to whistle, the city below dark and silent, cold blue moonlight

lines.say: Rule two. In Korea, they say a whistle at night calls snakes into the house.
lines.img: a dark snake sliding slowly across the tiled floor of a modern apartment entryway at night, shoes by the door, a thin strip of hallway light

lines.say: Rule three. Not just snakes. Ghosts and bad spirits follow the sound in.
lines.img: a pale shadowy figure standing just inside a dim apartment living room at night, half hidden behind a curtain, faint moonlight from the balcony

lines.say: Rule four. In Japan, it's called yobue. In some regions, it calls the tengu. Or kidnappers.
lines.img: a narrow empty Japanese residential street at night, one flickering streetlight, a tall dark figure with a long nose silhouetted on a rooftop above

lines.say: Rule five. Your parents say it's just a story to keep you quiet at night.
lines.img: a mother tucking a child into bed in a dim modern bedroom, finger raised to her lips, the window behind them black

lines.say: So why is someone whistling outside your window tonight?
lines.img: a dark bedroom window seen from inside at night, curtains slightly parted, nothing visible outside but black trees and a faint pale shape

loop_back: The last line plays a whistle outside the window — which throws the viewer straight back to rule one: never whistle after dark (not even to answer it).

gumi.say: I never whistle after dark. Have you ever tried it?

source: A common taboo in Korea and Japan: whistling at night is said to call snakes, ghosts or bad spirits; in Japan it is called yobue, and in some regions it is said to summon tengu or kidnappers. Parents in both countries still use it to keep children quiet at night.
